native_result.query: How does the effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP compare between developing countries and countries in Sub-Saharan Africa?
native_result.HypoA: The effect of increasing education expenditure on per capita GDP is more pronounced in developing countries outside of Sub-Saharan Africa compared to those within it
native_result.HypoB: Across the 2011-2015 overlap window (the only years for which the outcome, GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$), is available for both the Sub-Saharan Africa (SSF) and Lower Middle Income (LMC) country groups in the World Bank panel), the within-period association between the education-expenditure variable, Adjusted savings: education expenditure (% of GNI) (EduShare), and log GNI per capita is markedly more favourable in Sub-Saharan Africa than in Lower Middle Income countries. On the overlap window the labor force participation rate total (% ages 15+) (LFPR), gross primary and secondary school enrollment (% gross), and the annual percentage growth in exports of goods and services (Exports growth) are all observed for both groups, but with only T = 5 years per group and a lag of log GNI per capita absorbed, those extra controls would saturate the design. The headline regression therefore reports the partial slope in a pooled OLS interaction model that conditions only on log GNI per capita lagged one year and a linear time trend, while the broader-controlled check is held out separately. The headline comparative statistic of record, the interaction coefficient on EduShare x is_LMC, where is_LMC is the Lower-Middle-Income group indicator, equals -0.282 with a HAC (Newey-West, maxlags=1) standard error of 0.077 (t = -3.65, p ~ 0.0003), so the LMC slope on log GNI per capita with respect to EduShare is significantly below the SSF slope by about 0.28 log points (roughly 28 percent at the level of GNI per capita) for every 1-percentage-point increase in the education-expenditure share. Decomposed into per-group partial slopes, the SSF slope is positive (+0.083) while the LMC slope is negative (-0.200), so the same increase in education-expenditure share coincides with relatively higher per-capita GNI in Sub-Saharan Africa and relatively lower per-capita GNI in Lower Middle Income over this window. The result is robust to adding the school enrollment, primary (% gross) control in a broader-controlled pool on N = 8 (interaction = -0.264, HAC SE = 0.059, t = -4.50, p < 0.001), and the sign is preserved in a first-differenced specification on N = 6 that drops the lag-of-y and absorbs the common trend via differencing (differential interaction on d_edu_share x is_LMC = -0.149, HAC SE = 0.088). Bivariate slopes on the same five overlap years are negative in both groups (LMC: -0.659 against EduShare at r = -0.96; SSF: -0.100 at r = -0.97) because, in both groups, the education-expenditure share has been drifting down while per-capita GNI has risen; the comparative claim above is the residual partial slope after the common linear trend and one-year persistence are absorbed. Sample sizes: N = 8 in the headline pooled regression, 4 per group after losing the first overlap year to the lag of log GNI per capita. This is a descriptive comparison on a very short overlap, not a causal estimate.
native_result.WorkflowB: Executed in Python (pandas, numpy, statsmodels) with no external data and only data/worldbank_education_gdp.csv. (1) Reshape wide WDI CSV (12 rows = 2 groups x 6 series x 41 years) to a per-(group, year) panel. (2) Built coverage table: LMC GNI per capita has 41/41 obs; SSF GNI per capita has 5/41 (2011-2015); exports growth and labor force participation have leading-edge gaps that bound earlier comparisons. (3) Outlier scan on Exports of goods and services (annual % growth) flagged Sub-Saharan Africa -43.29 in 2011 (on overlap but dropped by lag-of-y) and Sub-Saharan Africa +30.04 in 1999 (outside overlap). (4) The labor force participation rate total (% ages 15+), gross primary and secondary school enrollment (% gross), and exports growth are all observed for both groups in the 2011-2015 overlap, so they are available in the analytic frame, but they are NOT in the headline regression because including all four along with the lag, trend, EduShare, is_LMC, and the interaction would saturate the N=8 design; their controlled effect is examined instead in the broader-controlled robustness check. (5) Headline pooled OLS with interaction (N = 8, 4 per group after the lag): log(GNI_pc) ~ EduShare + is_LMC + EduShare*is_LMC + log_gni_lag + trend, with Newey-West HAC SEs (maxlags=1). Headline coefficient b3 on EduShare*is_LMC = -0.282 (HAC SE 0.077, t = -3.65), giving effective per-group partial slopes SSF = +0.083, LMC = -0.200. (6) Reported per-group transparency regressions (bivariate OLS at T=5 and a 2-parameter residualized fit). (7) Ran two robustness checks: a broader-controlled pool adding gross primary enrollment (N=8, interaction = -0.264, HAC SE = 0.059) and a first-differenced specification that drops the lag (N=6, differential interaction = -0.149, HAC SE = 0.088). Per binding decision A3, pre-2011 LMC- and SSF-only descriptives are context only, never the comparative claim; per binding decision A1, EduShare (% of GNI) is the education-expenditure variable used (no dollar-spending substitution). Limitations: T = 5 overlap, N = 2 groups, descriptive not causal, bounded share, possible reverse causality, raw bivariate sign disagrees with trend-adjusted sign because both series trend in opposite directions, broader controls can only be examined one at a time at this sample size. Alignment note appended to workflow_and_hypothesis.md confirming that the headline regression conditions only on log_gni_lag and the linear trend, with broader controls held to the robustness check.
